subjectLine: GLP-1s don't strip muscle faster than dieting 💊
borisTake: This is the kind of result practitioners actually need: less panic, more protocol discipline. I'd still pair every GLP-1 cycle with resistance training and aggressive protein intake, but this paper makes the 'GLP-1s automatically melt your muscle' line look too sloppy.
leadAnalysis: The key mechanism here is that GLP-1-driven weight loss seems to follow the same basic tissue economics as ordinary caloric deficit: most mass comes off as fat, while the lean-mass component is partly non-muscle tissue such as liver and water-rich organs rather than catastrophic contractile loss. That matters because a lot of the public fear came from reading lean body mass as if it were synonymous with functional muscle. In the mouse datasets, absolute strength dipped a bit but strength relative to body weight improved, which is exactly what you'd expect if metabolic load is falling faster than useful tissue. Clinically, this shifts the conversation from 'avoid GLP-1s because of sarcopenia' to 'use them intelligently, then defend muscle with lifting, protein, and follow-up body-composition checks.'
oneNumber: 25% | Approximate share of GLP-1 weight loss that was lean mass, in line with ordinary dieting

papers.title: GLP-1 Drugs’ Muscle Effects Similar to Ordinary Weight Loss
papers.summary: A new analysis argues GLP-1 agonists do not appear to deplete muscle beyond what you'd expect from standard calorie-deficit weight loss, with roughly a quarter of lost weight coming from lean mass rather than the alarming 40% headline some people fixated on. More important, functional readouts held up well, which suggests the real job in clinic is protecting muscle during weight loss, not treating GLP-1s as uniquely sarcopenic.

papers.title: Forever Healthy Releases AI4L 1.0 for Practical Longevity
papers.summary: Forever Healthy launched AI4L, an open-source audit-driven system meant to generate and self-audit longevity intervention reviews against a 390-plus-point quality checklist with live citation checks. This is more tooling than wet-lab biology, but if it works, it could seriously compress the time needed to keep evidence reviews on rapamycin, NAD restoration, senolytics, and related protocols current.

papers.title: Towards a Context-Aware Framework for Cellular Senescence
papers.summary: This review pushes back on the lazy idea that senescence is one fixed endpoint with one universal biomarker set, arguing instead for a spectrum of senescent states that varies by tissue, stressor, timing, and disease context. For anyone building senolytics or senomorphic protocols, that means the field probably wins by getting more specific, not by pretending one drug or one marker can fit every senescent cell in the body.

papers.title: Celastrol as an Exercise Mimetic to Modestly Slow Aging
papers.summary: Researchers identified celastrol as a compound that mimics PGC-1α and exercise-like transcriptional programs, improving mitochondrial metabolism and muscle phenotypes across myoblasts, accelerated-aging mice, and C. elegans. The eye-catching figure is a 27.6% lifespan extension in worms, but the more believable translational angle is support for muscle energetics rather than any miracle anti-aging pill.

papers.title: Aging Sets the Stage for Respiratory Dysfunction and Disease
papers.summary: A new review lays out how autophagy decline, cellular senescence, chronic inflammation, and weaker airway defenses make the aging lung more vulnerable to COPD, fibrosis, infection, and sleep apnea. The practical message is that respiratory aging is under-measured but probably far more central to late-life risk than the field usually treats it.

papers.title: A Review of Mechanistic Links Between Obesity and Alzheimer’s Disease
papers.summary: The review catalogs a pretty convincing mechanistic bridge between obesity and Alzheimer’s biology, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, adipokine disruption, and systemic inflammation. But the epidemiology still refuses to give a clean one-to-one story, which is a useful reminder that plausible mechanisms do not automatically translate into a strong clinical risk model.

papers.title: Oxidative Stress Impairs Deubiquitylase Activity in the Aging Brain
papers.summary: Using activity-based proteomics, researchers found that several brain deubiquitylases lose catalytic activity with age despite stable abundance, linking oxidative stress to an early collapse in proteostasis control. NACET restored some of that activity, which makes this an interesting redox-plus-proteostasis node to watch in neurodegeneration.
